title: Stage Left, Stage Right
tagline: Control the stage before the scene controls you.
premise: Two stage crews compete to control a runaway play. Each turn, place a real theatre thing that handles the thing currently onstage: a curtain can hide a spotlight, and a spotlight can expose a curtain. The host gives a dry review of every failed bit of stagecraft.

tests: A stranger pictures the theatre thing at once. Nothing abstract, invented, or dependent on a famous show.
A non-player names a plain theatre counter within five seconds. Say what that counter is.
It can directly handle what stands onstage by blocking, revealing, trapping, silencing, removing, or controlling it. Merely being nearby is not stagecraft.
It makes a stranger want to answer with another theatre thing. A curtain, cue light, trapdoor, or prop is useful; a vague mood is not.
The wording uses everyday theatre words a twelve-year-old can understand. No proper show titles, actor names, brands, jargon, or dramatic speeches.

move_constraints.example: I am a blackout, and I swallow the spotlight.
move_constraints.hint: Name a theatre thing and its plain action on the standing thing.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and decisively the theatre thing controls what is currently onstage.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no action on the standing thing; 1 = a loose association or uncertain effect; 2 = a possible but incomplete bit of stagecraft; 3 = clear, direct control that handles the standing thing; 4 = total and immediate control, with no practical escape (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can picture the theatre thing and the action it performs.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable or self-contradicting; 1 = requires specialist theatre knowledge; 2 = understandable but hazy or overcomplicated; 3 = clear and concrete; 4 = instantly stageable and vivid (rare). Length never wins on its own: every extra word must clarify the bit.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How fresh the move is within the theatre, rather than a routine repeat of the same stage function.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the obvious repeat, a larger copy, or the same theatre function as the previous move; 2 = a sound but familiar stage solution; 4 = a surprising jump to a different part of theatre that still directly controls the standing thing (rare).

criterion.description: A move wins only when the named theatre thing directly blocks, reveals, traps, silences, removes, or otherwise controls what stands. Merely moving away, enduring it, waiting for it, or using a larger version of it loses.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the host, about the game, or about rules is itself a failed piece of stagecraft.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous theatre thing: judge the move against the opening card instead. It must plausibly handle or control the opening thing.
A larger, brighter, louder, or faster version of the standing thing is not a counter. A close cousin from the same stage function is also not enough unless it has a direct new action.
Becoming the opening thing itself, or a lightly changed copy of it, is a duplicate and fails the novelty gate.
Strength is measured against the standing theatre thing, never in the abstract. A theatre object that has no way to act on what stands fails, however useful it might be elsewhere.

The mechanism must be literal and stageable. A stranger should be able to watch the new theatre thing act on the standing one. A spotlight exposing a curtain is literal; applause defeating a problem is not.
Surviving, ignoring, avoiding, or waiting out the standing thing is not control. A costume that stays away from a trapdoor has not handled the trapdoor.
A move must name a real theatre thing, not a player, rule, review, idea, or plot event disguised as stage equipment.
A move that merely changes location does not win. Moving a spotlight to another corner does not control the spotlight already standing.
A move that claims control without naming what the theatre thing does fails. The host needs a visible stage action, not a confident announcement.

examples.mechanism: a blackout removes the light from the spotlight

examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, it avoids the spotlight instead of controlling it
examples.mechanism: none, waiting backstage does not act on the spotlight

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger should see the stage action from the two forms.
Name both theatre things, or plain stand-ins for them.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, or Move refused.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Use commas and full stops.
Use a deadpan review voice with mild playful jabs. Tease the failed stagecraft, never identity or personal traits.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, theatre quotes, profanity, or grand speeches.
On a refusal, explain the missing stage action and ask for another form. Do not declare a winner.
The coaching line names one theatre thing that would have handled the standing thing. End on an action or fact, not a mood or verdict.
Light innuendo is allowed only when it stays harmless and does not target a person.
good_headlines: The blackout swallowed the spotlight. Efficient, if not cheerful.
The stage manager turned the blackout back on. The dark has been given notes.
The follow spot exposed the curtain, which is awkward for a curtain.
The trapdoor removed the actor. The floor has made its point.
The bell called the cast, then the sound booth cut it off.
The prop table caught the rolling mask. At last, a prop with timing.
A larger bell is still a bell. Bring something that handles it.
The costume rack waited backstage while the spotlight did nothing to it. Bring another form.
The curtain is not defeated by standing near it. Try a spotlight.
The stage crew brought a cue sheet to a trapdoor. Paper remains above ground.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the blackout wins the spotlight.
The House Manager refuses: the bell was not persuasive.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, the costume rack is shy.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and gives no stage mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The trapdoor defeats the actor, the curtain, the audience, and perhaps the economy.
bad_headlines.why: adds unrelated claims and loses the plain reason
no reason and no useful stage picture

bad_headlines.text: A brave effort from someone who clearly cannot stage a scene.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player rather than the form

bad_headlines.text: The prop table, in a most operatic triumph, doth silence the bell.
The curtain was defeated, overcome, vanquished, and thoroughly bested.
bad_headlines.why: repeats one idea without showing an action

bad_headlines.text: The costume rack avoids the spotlight with admirable dignity.

rules: Handle the theatre thing in front of you. Do not merely leave the stage.
Say what you are and what you do to it: "I am a blackout, and I swallow the spotlight."
Use a real theatre thing and a plain, visible stage action.
The Judge rules on the idea, never the spelling.
One move that fails to control the standing thing ends the show.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next stage move while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the stage. Place a theatre thing.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A stage move, not a full rehearsal.
validation_messages.duplicate: That theatre thing already stood this show. Bring on something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Handle {standing_form}. Do not repeat it or simply step away.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two stage crews trying to control a runaway play.
Always use this shape: "I am [theatre thing], and I [plain action] the [standing thing]."
Good: "I am a blackout, and I swallow the spotlight." / "I am a spotlight, and I expose the curtain."
Bad: "I am a costume rack, and I wait backstage" because waiting does not control anything.
Bad: "I am a bigger spotlight, and I shine harder" because size and volume are not a new mechanism.
Use real theatre things anyone can picture: curtains, lights, bells, trapdoors,
props, costumes, ropes, scenery, cue lights, sound booths, and stage managers.
Theatre jargon is not a prize. Plain words beat clever speeches.
You are not performing for the audience and you are not joking. You are trying to
keep control of the stage. If a move lands funny, it is because the stage action is
clear and the failing thing has nowhere useful to stand.
Hop around the theatre: the stage, backstage, the booth, the dressing room,
the balcony, the loading dock. A fresh place is useful only if the thing there
acts directly on what stands.
Never reuse a theatre thing or an attribute from this match.
default_move: I am a curtain, and I hide the standing thing.
